title: Crème Caramel
subtitle: Baked vanilla custard with caramel sauce
excerpt: Individual baked vanilla custards set in a coating of dark caramel, unmoulded to reveal a trembling, golden-glazed dessert. One of the most technically satisfying of French puddings to make, and one of the most impressive to serve.
sourceNotes: Crème caramel is one of the defining desserts of French classical cooking. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), establishes the method. The dish spread from France throughout the Iberian Peninsula (as flan) and into Latin America during the colonial period, making it one of the most widely eaten desserts in the world. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the full method with detailed caramel instructions. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), notes that the dish is particularly associated with restaurant cooking rather than domestic kitchens.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 4 hours ahead; overnight is better. Keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Run a knife around the edge and unmould just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sugar heated until it melts and turns golden to amber, undergoing chemical reactions (caramelisation and Maillard reactions) that produce its characteristic deep, slightly bitter sweetness. The colour range runs from pale gold (140°C) to dark amber (175°C). For crème caramel, a dark amber caramel is used — if it is too pale it will taste only of sweet, without the depth that balances the rich custard.

content.text: Crème caramel has two distinct stages: first, a dark

is poured into the base of each ramekin and allowed to set; then a vanilla custard is poured on top and the whole is baked in a bain-marie. When the set custard is unmoulded, the caramel, which has liquefied again during the chilling period, floods over the custard as a sauce. The key is making the caramel dark enough: a pale caramel will make the finished dish sickly sweet.

Combine 150 g sugar and 4 tbsp water in the saucepan over medium heat. Do not stir, swirl the pan only. Cook until the caramel turns a deep amber colour and smells of toffee (about 175°C). Immediately divide among the 6 ramekins, tilting each to coat the base evenly. The caramel will harden as it cools. Set the ramekins in the roasting tin.
Warm the milk with the vanilla until steaming.
Whisk the whole eggs, egg yolks, and 80 g sugar together gently, do not create foam. Pour the warm milk onto the egg mixture in a thin stream, stirring gently. Strain through a fine sieve.
Pour the custard carefully over the set caramel in each ramekin, filling to within 5 mm of the top. Pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins.
Bake at 160°C for 30 to 35 minutes until the custard is just set, the edges should be firm but the centre should still wobble. Remove from the water bath, cool, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours.

To unmould: run a thin knife around the inside edge of each ramekin. Place a dessert plate upside-down on top and invert in one confident movement. The caramel sauce will flow around the custard. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The caramel will not unmould from the base of the ramekin
items.cause: The caramel has not had enough time to liquefy during chilling, or the ramekin was not run properly with the knife.
items.fix: Run the knife firmly all the way around the edge of the ramekin, pressing against the glass or porcelain. Dip the base of the ramekin into hot water for 5 seconds to soften the caramel. Invert confidently without hesitating.

items.cause: The custard was cooked at too high a temperature, causing the egg proteins to scramble.
items.fix: Keep the oven at 160°C fan maximum and use the bain-marie. The internal temperature of a correctly baked custard should not exceed 82°C.

items.symptom: The caramel tasted burnt rather than bitter-sweet
items.cause: The caramel was taken too dark.
items.fix: Watch the caramel carefully as it approaches the colour of dark amber. At 175°C it should smell of caramel rather than burnt sugar. The moment the colour is right, pour immediately, it continues to cook from residual heat.

content.text: Crème caramel spread from France to Spain, where it is called flan, and then to Portugal, Brazil, and much of the world. It is now one of the most widely eaten desserts across multiple continents. Each version differs slightly: the French original has a strong, dark caramel and a firm custard; the Spanish flan is often richer and sweeter; the Latin American version is thicker, usually made with condensed milk. The French original remains the reference point for the others.
